propositions.text: The appellants appealed a Federal Court decision dismissing judicial review of the Minister's decision.
The respondent moves to strike the appeal as moot.
The appellants oppose the motion to strike the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants appealed a Federal Court decision; the respondent moves to strike the appeal as moot, opposed by the appellants.

propositions.text: The Minister's decision added a requirement that applicants attest their job and mandate respect human rights including reproductive rights.
The attestation specifically referenced reproductive rights and the 2018 CSJ Applicant Guide explained human rights include reproductive rights and abortion access.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister's decision required attestation respecting human rights including reproductive rights, as explained in the 2018 CSJ Applicant Guide.

propositions.text: The appellant TRTL did not make the attestation but submitted a letter objecting to it and offered an alternative attestation.
The Minister declined to consider TRTL's application as incomplete for lacking the required attestation, so TRTL received no funding in 2018.
Appellants include TRTL, Blaise Alleyne (former president), and Matthew Battista (student hoping for summer employment).

paragraphs.summary: TRTL did not make the attestation but objected and offered an alternative; the Minister declined to consider the application, so TRTL got no funding; appellants include TRTL, Alleyne, and Battista.

propositions.text: The appellants sought judicial review of the Decision, declarations of Charter infringement, ultra vires, bad faith, and mandamus ordering funding.
The appellants did not seek judicial review of the decision not to review TRTL's application or deny funding.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants sought judicial review and declarations but not review of the refusal to consider TRTL's application or deny funding.

propositions.text: The Federal Court found the Decision reasonable, not ultra vires, not made in bad faith or improper purpose.
The Federal Court found TRTL's section 15 Charter rights not engaged, section 2(a) and 2(b) engaged but justified under section 1 as minimal limitation.
The Federal Court found the limitation proportionate balancing freedoms and program objectives.
The Federal Court found Alleyne had standing but Battista did not.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found the Decision reasonable, Charter rights mostly justified, and Alleyne had standing but Battista did not.

propositions.text: The appellants assert the Federal Court erred on section 15 rights, section 2 limitations, closed mind, and Battista's standing.
The steps to set the appeal for hearing are complete.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants assert errors in the Federal Court's Charter and standing findings; appeal hearing steps are complete.

propositions.text: The respondent moves to strike the appeal as moot due to no live controversy; attestation removed in 2019 and 2018 program concluded.
The appellants do not dispute the attestation removal fact noted in Redeemer University case.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent moves to strike the appeal as moot citing attestation removal and program conclusion; appellants do not dispute removal fact.

propositions.text: The appellants argue mootness should have been raised earlier and not on appeal as a new issue.
The court disagrees and states mootness may be raised anytime, even by the court itself, citing CUPE and Hakizimana.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue mootness raised too late; the court disagrees, allowing mootness to be raised anytime, citing precedent.

propositions.text: The first question is whether the appeal is moot.
If moot, the court must decide whether to exercise discretion to hear appeal using Borowski factors.

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if the appeal is moot and if so, whether to hear it using Borowski factors.

propositions.text: The judicial review subject was the Decision adding the attestation to the 2018 CSJ application, not the refusal to consider TRTL's application or alternative attestation.

paragraphs.summary: The judicial review concerned the Decision adding the attestation, not the refusal to consider TRTL's application or alternative attestation.

propositions.text: The 2018 CSJ program ended and the attestation was removed from the 2019 application form.
Reviewing the Decision's reasonableness will not serve a useful purpose as it is overtaken by events.

paragraphs.summary: The 2018 program ended and attestation removed in 2019; reviewing the Decision now serves no useful purpose.

propositions.text: The appellants say the appeal is not moot because they seek a Charter breach declaration, citing Trang 2005.
TRTL concedes the core remedy sought is a declaration of Charter breach in 2018.
The court may make binding declarations but whether to do so depends on circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue appeal not moot due to Charter breach declaration sought; court notes declarations depend on circumstances.

propositions.text: A Charter breach declaration may only be granted if it has practical utility and settles a live controversy, citing Daniels, Solosky, and Income Security Advocacy Centre.

paragraphs.summary: A Charter breach declaration requires practical utility and a live controversy, per precedent.

propositions.text: A declaration that Charter rights were violated in a spent program serves no practical utility or live controversy.
Future similar attestation requirements can be challenged then, depending on their nature and reasons.
A decision here likely would be of no use in a future case with different facts.

paragraphs.summary: A declaration about a spent program has no practical utility; future challenges can be made if similar attestations arise.

propositions.text: Trang 2007 states declarations may not be granted if dispute is academic or has no practical effect, overturning a lower court declaration.
Declarations rarely granted if no practical effect on parties' rights, per Trang 2007.

paragraphs.summary: Trang 2007 holds declarations not granted if dispute is academic or has no practical effect; declarations rarely granted without practical effect.

propositions.text: Utility of a declaration depends on other available remedies.
Here, only mandamus ordering funding would make relief practically useful.

paragraphs.summary: Declaration utility depends on other remedies; here only mandamus ordering funding would have practical utility.

propositions.text: Mandamus is discretionary and requires satisfying eight criteria from Apotex or severe maladministration cases like LeBon and D'Errico.
Appellants have not addressed mandamus criteria in any materials.
Record shows no basis for mandamus, supporting view that Charter breach declaration lacks practical utility.

paragraphs.summary: Mandamus requires criteria not addressed by appellants; record shows no basis, supporting no practical utility for declaration.

propositions.text: Even if TRTL's 2018 application was processed, funding was not certain due to oversubscription and priorities excluding TRTL's mandate.
Federal Court found funding was not certain given eligibility criteria and priorities.
Mandamus granted only where outcome on merits is foregone conclusion, citing D'Errico and Doyle.

paragraphs.summary: Funding was uncertain due to oversubscription and priorities; mandamus granted only if outcome is foregone conclusion.

propositions.text: Mandamus claim insufficient to render appeal not moot; appeal is moot.

paragraphs.summary: Mandamus claim insufficient; the appeal is moot.

propositions.text: Court considers whether to hear moot appeal using Borowski factors: adversarial context, practical utility, and proper role of court.
Borowski factors guide discretion to hear moot appeals; no single factor is determinative.

paragraphs.summary: Court will consider Borowski factors to decide whether to hear moot appeal; no factor alone is determinative.

propositions.text: There is an adversarial context in this case.
Issues were fully argued before the Federal Court with submissions from two interveners.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds there is an adversarial context and that issues were fully argued before the Federal Court with interveners' submissions.

propositions.text: The 2018 CSJ program is expired and the impugned attestation was removed in 2019.
A moot appeal should not be heard based on mere speculation the same issue may arise again (Hakizimana at para. 22).
There is no suggestion the same issue will arise again.
If the same issue arises in the future, it is not necessarily evasive of court review.
Examples include Redeemer University, BCM International Canada Inc. v. Canada, and Right to Life Association of Toronto and Area v. Canada (Employment, Workforce and Labour).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 2018 CSJ program expired, moot appeal should not be heard on speculation, no suggestion issue will recur, and future issues are not necessarily evasive of review.

propositions.text: Judicial review can be an effective remedy for Charter breaches and may proceed more quickly than damages actions.
The CSJ application form was changed after 2018.
Effectiveness of judicial review does not mean this appeal should be heard.
Court should not make declarations assuming 2018 circumstances may recur (Fibrogen, Inc. v. Akebia Therapeutics, Inc.).
If application process changes yearly, deciding now lacks an existing factual matrix (Hakizimana at para. 19).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds judicial review effective but this appeal should not be heard due to changed facts and lack of current factual matrix.

propositions.text: The Court should hear the appeal because the Federal Court decision will be binding precedent immune from appellate review.
Appellants’ interest is jurisprudential, insufficient to sustain a moot appeal (CUPE at para. 7).
Such argument could be made in any moot appeal and cannot alone determine hearing the appeal.
A decision here may have no jurisprudential impact as future programs may differ.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the appeal should be heard to avoid binding precedent; the court finds this interest insufficient and the decision may lack jurisprudential impact.

propositions.text: Raising a constitutional question alone does not justify hearing an appeal unless social cost of uncertainty outweighs judicial economy (Abel v. Canada).
The court is not convinced social cost here outweighs judicial economy given the CSJ program nature and issues.

paragraphs.summary: The court states constitutional questions alone do not justify hearing appeals unless social cost outweighs judicial economy, which is not shown here.

propositions.text: Hearing the appeal would be making law in the abstract since the impugned attestation is removed.
Creating legal precedent in a case with no practical consequences is improper law-making (CUPE at para. 13).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds hearing the appeal would be abstract law-making, which is improper, given no practical consequences remain.

propositions.text: The Court should not hear this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes it should not hear the appeal.

propositions.text: This appeal is moot and the Court should not exercise discretion to hear it.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the appeal is moot and should not be heard.

propositions.text: The respondent seeks costs of $800 for this motion.
The appellants were silent on the issue of costs.
The court would not award any costs and notes respondent should have brought the motion sooner.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent seeks costs; appellants silent; the court declines costs and criticizes respondent's delay.

propositions.text: Respondent was originally named as Canada (Minister of Employment, Workforce, and Labour).
Under Federal Court Rules, the proper respondent is the Attorney General of Canada.
This change is a matter of form and does not affect the motion outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the proper respondent is the Attorney General of Canada, a formality not affecting the motion outcome.

propositions.text: The style of cause is amended to reflect the Attorney General of Canada as sole respondent.
The motion to strike the appeal for mootness is granted and the appeal is dismissed without costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court amends the style of cause, grants the motion to strike for mootness, and dismisses the appeal without costs.
